findings.message: The PR replaced the L2-cache justification with 'batched within a single transaction', which is inaccurate in two ways. First, @BatchSize(20) is a Hibernate session-level optimisation, not a transaction-level one. Second, with spring.jpa.open-in-view: false and no @Transactional on this controller, each repository call opens its own short-lived session, so there is no shared session in which batching across multiple user loads can occur. For single-user GET endpoints — the common case — @BatchSize provides no benefit. Previously, User.authorities were served from the L2 entity cache after the first call; now every HTTP call that touches authorities pays the database round-trip unconditionally. The comment tells developers the N+1 is 'handled' by @BatchSize when it is not, likely causing the real regression to go unaddressed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The comment introduced by this PR says @BatchSize batches 'within a single transaction', but @BatchSize is a session-level optimization, not transaction-level. With spring.jpa.open-in-view: false (confirmed in application.yml), each repository call has its own session, so for single-user GET endpoints @BatchSize provides no N+1 mitigation. The term 'transaction' is factually wrong, and the comment overstates the mitigation provided.
findings.severity_justification: This is primarily a comment inaccuracy introduced by this PR. No runtime behavior is changed by the comment itself; the real concern is documentation misleading developers about the effectiveness of @BatchSize, which has always been there. The N+1 issue itself is pre-existing.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about a factually inaccurate code comment that uses 'transaction' instead of 'session' and overstates how @BatchSize mitigates N+1 queries in this specific architecture.

findings.message: Same inaccuracy as UserResource.java: the PR replaced the L2-cache rationale with 'batched within a single transaction', but @BatchSize is per Hibernate session and this controller has no @Transactional. With open-in-view: false there is no shared session across repository calls within a request, so @BatchSize(20) does not batch authority loads in the typical single-user lookup. Every HTTP call that touches User.authorities now unconditionally hits the database. The comment misrepresents the performance behaviour and creates a false sense that the N+1 problem is resolved.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The same inaccurate comment from Finding 1 appears verbatim in AdminUserResource.java at lines 78-81. It says @BatchSize batches 'within a single transaction' when @BatchSize is session-scoped, not transaction-scoped. With open-in-view: false confirmed, there is no shared session across repository calls, making the comment misleading for single-user lookups.
findings.severity_justification: Same as Finding 1 — this is a comment inaccuracy introduced by the PR. No runtime behavior is changed by the comment; the N+1 issue and @BatchSize behavior pre-exist this PR.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about an inaccurate code comment using 'transaction' instead of 'session', overstating the mitigation provided by @BatchSize in this architecture.

findings.message: Stale Javadoc comment: 'The user cache is properly evicted for all affected users.' This was made incorrect by this PR's changes to UserService.removeGroupFromAllUsers(), which removed the pre-fetch of affected user logins and the subsequent per-login cache eviction loop. The method now performs no cache eviction at all. The comment misleads maintainers of unenrollStudentsTutorsAndEditors() into believing stale-cache handling is present when it is not.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The comment at line 493 of CourseResetService.java says 'The user cache is properly evicted for all affected users.' Verified that UserService.removeGroupFromAllUsers() now only calls userRepository.removeGroupFromAllUsers() and logs — there is no cache eviction. This PR removed the eviction methods but left this comment stale, making it factually incorrect.
findings.severity_justification: With Hibernate L2 disabled cluster-wide and no Spring @Cacheable on User entities, there is currently no user cache to evict, so the stale comment causes no runtime issue. The risk is maintainers being misled into thinking eviction is handled if a new cache is introduced later.
findings.category_justification: This is a stale Javadoc comment that became incorrect when the PR removed the cache eviction logic it describes, misleading maintainers about the actual behavior of unenrollStudentsTutorsAndEditors().

findings.message: USERS_CACHE = "users" is now dead production code. No @Cacheable annotation in production code uses the cache name "users", and the clearUserCaches() methods removed by this PR used User.class.getName() as the key — not this constant. The constant is only referenced in UserTestService.java:141 where it evicts a cache that is never populated, making the eviction a silent no-op. Leaving the constant in UserRepository creates the false impression that a live Spring 'users' cache exists and must be evicted around writes, which could lead future contributors to add incorrect eviction logic.
findings.tp_fp_justification: USERS_CACHE = "users" at line 71 is confirmed dead production code — no @Cacheable annotation in production code uses the name "users". It is only referenced in UserTestService.java:141 where it evicts a cache that is never populated. The constant pre-existed this PR but was already dead. The PR, as a cache cleanup effort, was the natural time to remove it and did not.
findings.severity_justification: Dead constant with no runtime impact. Risk is future contributors seeing it and adding incorrect eviction logic, but this is speculative. No current functionality is affected.
findings.category_justification: Dead code (an unused constant) that misleads maintainers about the existence of a live 'users' Spring cache, with no runtime impact.

findings.message: The method `removeGroupFromAllUsers` performs a bulk update to remove a group from users, but it no longer evicts the affected users from the cache. While the Hibernate L2 cache for `User` entities has been removed, Spring's `CacheManager` might still be in use for user-related data (e.g., via `@Cacheable` on other services). The removal of `findLoginsByGroupName` and the cache eviction logic could lead to stale data if other user-related caches exist.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding speculates that Spring @Cacheable might cache user-related data affected by group removal. Investigation shows no Spring @Cacheable in production code caches user group membership. All existing Spring caches (titles, files, notification settings, saved posts) are keyed independently of group membership and are not invalidated by removeGroupFromAllUsers — correctly so, since they don't depend on group data. The claim is unverifiable speculation rather than an identified concrete issue.
findings.severity_justification: Even if taken at face value, the finding describes a hypothetical risk with no identified concrete cache that would actually become stale.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about stale cache data leading to incorrect behavior after group membership changes.

findings.message: The method `deleteUser` no longer calls `clearUserCaches`. While the primary L2 cache for `User` entities was removed, this might affect other caches related to users if they exist (e.g. through Spring's `@Cacheable`). A user deleted from the database could persist in other caches, leading to stale data.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding speculates that 'other caches related to users might exist' without identifying any specific cache. As confirmed in Finding 5, no Spring @Cacheable caches user identity or group membership data that would be accessed after deletion. Notification/saved-post caches keyed by userId would hold orphaned entries, but a deleted user's auth tokens are invalid so no live request could access those stale cache entries.
findings.severity_justification: Even if accepted, the described scenario — stale cache entries for a deleted user — has no practical impact since deleted users cannot authenticate.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about stale cache data for deleted users potentially being accessed.

findings.message: The `saveUser` method no longer clears user-related caches. While the Hibernate L2 entity cache for `User` is gone, other caches might exist (e.g. DTOs cached with Spring's `@Cacheable`). If so, updating a user will not evict their previous state from those caches, leading to stale data being served.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Same speculative concern as Findings 5 and 6. No Spring @Cacheable in production code caches user identity or attribute data that would become stale on a saveUser() call. The finding says 'other caches might exist' without identifying any specific cache — it is unverifiable speculation rather than a concrete issue.
findings.severity_justification: No specific cache is identified; the concern is hypothetical and not supported by the actual @Cacheable usage in the codebase.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about stale cached user data being served after a user update.

findings.message: The loop iterating over distributed objects to bind cache metrics now only considers `IMap`. Previously, it also handled `javax.cache.Cache` (ICache) instances for JCache/L2 metrics. While L2 is disabled, it's possible for `ICache` instances to be used for other purposes. If any `ICache` instances are still in use, their metrics will no longer be bound to Micrometer.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The javax.cache:cache-api and hibernate-jcache dependencies are completely removed from build.gradle, and there are no remaining ICache or javax.cache usages anywhere in production code. The finding speculates ICache instances 'might' be used for other purposes, but in this codebase they were exclusively for Hibernate L2. No ICache instances can exist at runtime.
findings.severity_justification: Even if accepted, this would only affect metrics visibility, not correctness or reliability.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about metrics not being bound to Micrometer if ICache instances existed, which is an operational observability concern.

The comment now explains the two deletion paths in terms of Hibernate lazy-loading, FK constraints, and @PreRemove — no L2 cache mention remains.

findings.category_justification: The concern is about stale/misleading comments in method Javadoc.

findings.message: The removal of caching from the authorities association in User entities might lead to a higher overhead for authorization checks, which need frequent access to this collection.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While User.authorities is a hot path for authorization, Spring Security does not re-fetch user authorities from the database on every request — they are embedded in JWT tokens or stored in sessions. The finding provides no measured regression or hit rate data. It follows the same speculative pattern as Findings 12/16/17 — generic 'removing cache might hurt performance' applied to one of 116 annotation removals, which is exactly the PR's intentional design.
findings.severity_justification: No measured regression identified; Spring Security auth mechanisms typically avoid per-request DB reloads of authorities.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about performance overhead for authorization checks from cache removal.

findings.message: The added ArchUnit rule to prevent @Cache annotations does not verify the presence of adequate replacement strategies for removed caching logic.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding complains that the ArchUnit rule only enforces absence of @Cache without verifying replacement strategies. This contradicts the PR's documented policy: the default is 'do not cache', so no replacement is required. Requiring proof of a replacement would invert the policy. The rule is correctly scoped — it enforces the ban. The finding does not identify a concrete test gap or incorrect behavior.
findings.severity_justification: The finding describes an impossible or undesirable test requirement given the project's explicit policy that caching is opt-in with measured justification.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about the adequacy of the ArchUnit test coverage.
